exampleAnswers.Purpose and audience: A handover guide with deliverable locations, maintenance responsibilities, and recovery steps.
exampleAnswers.Working context: This fictional handover covers Greenhouse’s five-page website. The owner receives approved files and a short routine for keeping business information current. The index below uses descriptive locations rather than live private links.
exampleAnswers.Example records:
Item: Approved page set · Purpose: Published content reference · Owner: Café owner
Item: Brand folder · Purpose: Licensed logo and images · Owner: Studio lead
Item: Update guide · Purpose: Routine content changes · Owner: Café owner
Item: Review checklist · Purpose: Monthly quality check · Owner: Shift lead
exampleAnswers.Content decisions:
The first walkthrough: Open the home page on a phone and follow the paths to hours, the menu, and directions. Then use the update guide to identify where each item is maintained. Record anything the new owner cannot find.
Monthly maintenance: Check hours and menu information, test contact links, and review whether any images or copy have expired. Record the review date and the person who completed it.
When something goes wrong: Capture the affected page, the time, and what was expected. Contact the named support owner through the agreed channel. Keep a verified recovery procedure in the private handover; do not publish credentials.
exampleAnswers.Format and interaction: manual layout; section navigation and expandable detail where useful; matching portrait document PDF.
exampleAnswers.Sharing and provenance: A hypothetical example informed by Claw Me’s small-team and Agent workflows. These are not Pete’s actual clients, finances, travel plans, research results, or commitments. Keep the real adaptation private until the owner chooses to share.
